case_name: Flare-On 11 (2024) — CTF Malware Reverse Engineering Corpus
description: Flare-On 11 (2024) challenge corpus. Ten CTF reversing challenges distributed as a single ZIP containing individual 7z archives protected with CTF passwords. Challenges span a spectrum of adversarial techniques: array-based obfuscation (aray), BLAKE2 cryptographic keying (bloke2), ransomware (CatbertRansomware), ClearFake-style dropper (clearlyfake), a trojanized OpenSSH server (sshd), and additional RE puzzles. This corpus is used for forensic TTP classification and intentionality analysis training.

peirce_chain.firstness: ZIP archive containing 10 CTF challenge 7z files and a PASSWORD.txt. Challenge names self-describe the technique: 'CatbertRansomware', 'clearlyfake', 'sshd' (193 MB trojanized binary), 'serpentine', 'fullspeed'. The structure is consistent with a sanctioned reverse-engineering competition corpus.
peirce_chain.secondness: Challenge sizes are diagnostic. sshd.7z at 193 MB is anomalous for a CTF puzzle — consistent with a full trojanized SSH daemon binary, not a crafted crackme. CatbertRansomware.7z at 1.6 MB indicates a self-contained ransomware sample. clearlyfake.7z at 1.6 KB indicates a dropper stub, consistent with documented ClearFake campaign initial-access technique.
peirce_chain.thirdness: Each challenge encodes a deliberate adversarial technique requiring analyst knowledge of that TTP family to solve. The aggregate corpus constitutes a curated IoI (Indicator of Intent) training set covering T1486 (ransomware), T1566 (phishing/dropper), T1554 (compromised binaries), T1027 (obfuscation), T1140 (deobfuscation-keying via BLAKE2). The challenge designers deliberately selected real-world TTP archetypes.

devil_advocate: This is an authorized Mandiant/FLARE CTF educational corpus. No attacker infrastructure is active. The 'malware' samples are sandboxed CTF puzzles, not weaponized payloads. All files are 7z-password-protected and require participant-recovered passwords to execute. Forensic interest is taxonomic, not threat-response.

artifacts.description: Flare-On11_Challenges.zip — primary distribution archive. SHA-256 verified. Size 214,568,790 bytes. Contains 10 CTF challenge 7z files and PASSWORD.txt.

aray.7z (2,927 bytes) — array-based obfuscation challenge. Small size consistent with a crackme using array index arithmetic to obscure control flow or key derivation. TTP: T1027 (obfuscated files/information).

bloke2.7z (5,775 bytes) — BLAKE2 cryptographic hash-based challenge. Name is wordplay on BLAKE2 algorithm. Likely uses custom BLAKE2 implementation for key derivation or license check. TTP: T1140 (deobfuscate/decode files).

CatbertRansomware.7z (1,692,864 bytes) — ransomware sample. Largest text-challenge entry aside from sshd. Name references Dilbert character Catbert (evil HR director), consistent with Mandiant/FLARE humor. Self-contained ransomware binary. TTP: T1486 (data encrypted for impact).

metadata.inferred_technique: file encryption ransomware, likely AES or ChaCha20 with asymmetric key wrapping

artifacts.description: checksum.7z (1,392,978 bytes) — checksum-based integrity or key derivation challenge. Name implies the binary computes or validates a checksum as part of its protection scheme. TTP: T1140 (deobfuscate/decode files or information).

clearlyfake.7z (1,616 bytes) — ClearFake-style dropper. Extremely small size (1.6 KB) consistent with a JavaScript dropper or PowerShell stub, matching the documented ClearFake campaign that distributes fake browser updates. TTP: T1566.001 (spearphishing attachment / fake update dropper).

metadata.inferred_technique: ClearFake fake-browser-update dropper, JavaScript or PowerShell initial stage

artifacts.description: frog.7z (10,653,489 bytes) — challenge of moderate size. Name suggests obfuscation or game-engine challenge (10 MB consistent with Unity or similar runtime). TTP: T1027 (obfuscated files/information).

metadata.inferred_technique: game engine or runtime-embedded crackme, possible Unity IL2CPP

artifacts.description: fullspeed.7z (771,776 bytes) — name suggests a speed-optimization or crypto challenge. 'Full speed' may reference elliptic curve cryptography (FullSpeed EC variant) or a timing-dependent protection. TTP: T1027 (obfuscation via cryptographic technique).

metadata.inferred_technique: elliptic curve or modular arithmetic-based protection (possible FullSpeed EC)

artifacts.description: mememaker3000.7z (1,010,226 bytes) — name suggests a social engineering or steganography-themed challenge, possibly hiding flags in images or using meme-format payloads. TTP: T1027.003 (steganography) or T1059 (scripting).

metadata.inferred_technique: steganography in image or web-based meme generator with embedded payload

artifacts.description: serpentine.7z (5,725,299 bytes) — name references serpentine/snake motion, possibly Python-based challenge or a challenge featuring serpentine data encoding. TTP: T1059.006 (Python) or T1027 (obfuscation).

metadata.inferred_technique: Python-based or serpentine encoding obfuscation challenge

artifacts.description: sshd.7z (193,244,435 bytes) — by far the largest challenge at 193 MB. Name and size are consistent with a full trojanized OpenSSH daemon. Real-world analog: XZ Utils/liblzma supply chain compromise (CVE-2024-3094). Challenge likely requires diffing or patching a modified sshd binary. TTP: T1554 (compromise software supply chain) and T1059 (command execution via backdoored daemon).

metadata.inferred_technique: trojanized sshd binary — supply chain compromise, analogous to XZ Utils CVE-2024-3094
